title: Asthma (Tamaka Shwasa): Ayurvedic View, Triggers, Diet & Care
excerpt: Breathlessness, chest tightness, wheezing and a cough that gets worse at night — these are common signs of asthma. Learn what asthma is, how Ayurveda understands it as “Tamaka Shwasa”, what sets off an attack, what to eat and avoid, pranayama, safe home measures and when you must go to hospital immediately.
content:
“As soon as winter comes, I get breathless at night and there is a whistling sound from my chest” — many people, children too, tell us this at the clinic. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), asthma affected an estimated 262 million people worldwide in 2019. Even if asthma is not completely “cured”, with the right treatment and care most people can live a normal, active life.

The most important point — do not stop the inhaler your doctor has given you on your own; Ayurvedic treatment is used alongside it as support. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is Asthma?

Asthma is a long-term disease of the breathing tubes (airways) of the lungs. On contact with a trigger (such as dust, smoke or cold air), three changes happen in these tubes:

  • Swelling — the inner lining of the tubes becomes inflamed
  • Muscle tightening — the muscles around the tubes tighten, narrowing the passage
  • More mucus — thick mucus forms and blocks the passage further

This is why breathing in and out becomes difficult. Asthma is not contagious; it can start in childhood or in later life. COPD caused by smoking and breathlessness due to a weak heart are different diseases, so do not treat every breathlessness as asthma on your own.

The Ayurvedic View

In Ayurveda, breathing disorders are called Shwasa Roga, and of its five types, Tamaka Shwasa most closely matches today’s asthma. Acharya Charaka describes how Shwasa develops:

यदा स्रोतांसि संरुध्य मारुतः कफपूर्वकः ।
विष्वग्व्रजति संरुद्धस्तदा श्वासान् करोति सः ॥
— Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 17

Meaning: When Vata (air), together with Kapha, blocks the channels of breathing and, being obstructed, spreads in all directions, it produces Shwasa (breathing disorders).

So in asthma, Kapha and Vata are the main doshas — Kapha blocks the passage and the obstructed air moves the wrong way, causing breathlessness. Ayurveda also says the root of Shwasa often lies in the amashaya (digestion), so weak agni, heavy food and constipation can also increase attacks. According to the texts, Tamaka Shwasa worsens with clouds, rain, cold, the east wind and Kapha-increasing food. It is considered a yapya disease — meaning it can be kept under control for a long time with regular care.

Main Causes and Triggers

  • Family history of asthma, allergy, sneezing (allergic rhinitis) or eczema
  • House dust and the tiny mites living in it, mould, cockroaches, pet hair and pollen
  • Bidi-cigarette smoke (including other people’s), smoke from chulhas, incense, mosquito coils, firecrackers and stubble burning; air pollution
  • Colds and viral infections, cold air and sudden weather changes
  • Strong smells (perfume, paint, chemicals), some medicines (such as certain painkillers) — always tell your doctor
  • Acidity (sour belching), obesity, stress, and heavy exercise without a warm-up

Symptoms and Tests

  • Breathlessness, especially at night or early morning
  • A whistling sound while breathing out (wheezing)
  • Tightness or heaviness in the chest
  • Repeated dry cough that worsens at night, in the cold or after exercise
  • In children, frequent “cold settling on the chest” or tiring quickly while playing
  • During an attack, being able to breathe only while sitting up, and difficulty speaking

For a correct diagnosis, the doctor tests with spirometry (lung function test) and a peak flow meter; if needed, a chest X-ray, blood tests or allergy tests may be advised. Keeping a peak flow diary at home helps you recognise an attack in advance. Be sure to get a written “asthma action plan” from your doctor — what to take daily and what to do during an attack.

Diet: What to Eat, What to Avoid

In asthma, the aim of diet is to keep agni healthy, not let Kapha increase, and keep the stomach light. According to Ayurveda, warm, fresh, light and easily digestible food is beneficial.

What to eat

  • Lukewarm water through the day, a little at a time
  • Old rice, wheat, barley, moong dal, horse gram — light, warm meals
  • Vegetables — bottle gourd, ridge gourd, pointed gourd, drumstick (moringa), fenugreek, spinach (well cooked)
  • Warm moong or vegetable soup with ginger, black pepper, cumin and turmeric
  • Seasonal fruit at room temperature, in the daytime — such as pomegranate, papaya, guava (if they suit you)
  • A light, early dinner — at least 2–3 hours before sleep

What to avoid

  • Fridge-cold water, ice cream, cold drinks and very cold foods
  • Curd (especially at night), heavy sweets, refined flour, fried food and junk food
  • Stale food, packaged foods with preservatives, and heavy late-night meals
  • Foods that give you allergy or an attack — identify and avoid them (they can differ from person to person)

Daily Routine and Home Environment

  • Allow no smoking at all in the house; avoid smoke from incense, dhoop, mosquito coils and chulhas
  • Wash bedsheets and pillow covers in hot water every week and dry them in the sun; mop with a wet cloth instead of sweeping
  • Cover your nose and mouth on polluted days and in cold wind; avoid walks in very cold early mornings
  • Keep washing hands to prevent colds; ask your doctor about vaccines such as flu
  • Exercise lightly every day, but warm up first; keep your weight under control
  • Sleep on time, don’t let constipation and acidity build up, and keep stress low

Yoga and Pranayama

Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari, slow deep belly breathing (diaphragmatic breathing), Ujjayi, and poses such as Bhujangasana, Setu Bandhasana, Marjari Asana and Sukhasana are considered helpful. Caution: do no pranayama or asana during an attack; do not do fast pranayama like Kapalabhati and Bhastrika with high blood pressure, heart disease, pregnancy or when breathless; learn yoga from a trained teacher and keep your reliever inhaler with you.

Safe Home Measures

  • Steam inhalation: plain hot-water steam for 5–10 minutes — helps loosen mucus; take special care against burns with children
  • Ginger-tulsi: a mild warm decoction of ginger and tulsi leaves, with a little honey if you like (never give honey to a child under one year)
  • Turmeric: turmeric in food; warm turmeric milk at night, if milk does not increase your mucus or discomfort
  • Keeping the chest warm: keep the chest and throat covered in winter; gargle with lukewarm water

These measures are only supportive — during an attack they cannot replace the reliever inhaler. If any herb or home item causes allergy, stop it immediately.

Ayurvedic Treatment — With Caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for Shwasa, such as Vasa (Adusa), Kantakari, Pippali, Pushkarmool, Haridra (turmeric), Tulsi, and classical formulations like Sitopaladi Churna and Agastya Haritaki. Acharya Charaka also describes applying oil to the chest followed by warm fomentation (Snehana-Swedana) for the Shwasa patient. After examination, when suitable, Nasya Karma, Panchakarma and personalised yoga-pranayama may be advised. However:

  • Which medicine or procedure, in what amount and for how long — this is decided by the vaidya only after looking at the stage of disease, age, constitution, pulse, triggers and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your inhaler, nebuliser or any current medicine on your own — inhalers are not “habit-forming”; they are a safe way to deliver medicine directly to the lungs. Any reduction in medicine only under your doctor’s supervision.
  • Some herbs (such as mulethi/liquorice) can affect blood pressure or other medicines, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines; avoid unlabelled “miracle asthma medicines” from the market — hidden steroids have sometimes been found in them.
  • During pregnancy and breastfeeding, and for children and the elderly, give any medicine only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “asthma cured from the root” or “you will be off inhalers forever”.

When to Go to Hospital Immediately

  • No relief even after using the reliever inhaler, or needing it again and again — go to a hospital immediately
  • Difficulty speaking a full sentence, or being unable to walk due to breathlessness
  • Blue lips or nails, extreme anxiety, drowsiness or confusion
  • In children, skin between the ribs or below the throat sinking in while breathing, or being unable to drink milk or water
  • Breathlessness with high fever, or chest pain
  • Peak flow less than half of your usual reading (if you use a peak flow meter)

Summary — Points to Remember

  • Asthma can be controlled — do not leave your inhaler and doctor’s advice on your own
  • Identify your triggers: smoke, dust, cold air, colds — and avoid them
  • Warm, light food; less cold food, curd (at night) and heavy meals
  • Regular pranayama and exercise, but not during an attack
  • Ayurvedic medicines and Panchakarma only under a qualified vaidya, as supportive treatment
